hints: Think of the two components that make up any complex, the electron deficient centre and the electron pair donors around it.
walkthrough:
Picture what a complex looks like**
Imagine a single metal ion in the middle, like $\text{Pt}^{4+}$, with molecules or ions clustered around it. Those surrounding species are using a lone pair to form a dative bond to the metal. That whole assembly is the complex.

Build the precise definition**
You need both halves for the mark: a central metal atom or ion, plus ligands surrounding it. A ligand is simply a species that donates a lone pair to form a co-ordinate bond, for example $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or $\text{CN}^-$.
Final answer: A central transition metal atom or ion surrounded by one or more ligands co-ordinately bonded to it.

hints: Count the total number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to Pt in each ion to get co-ordination number.
Use overall ion charge equals Pt oxidation number plus sum of ligand charges, remembering $\text{NH}_3$ is 0 and $\text{Cl}$ is -1.
walkthrough:
Count bonds for co-ordination number**
Co-ordination number is just the number of co-ordinate bonds to the metal, which equals the number of ligands here because all are monodentate. In $[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]^{2+}$ you have $4 + 2 = 6$ ligands bonded, so co-ordination number 6. In $[\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}$ you have 4 ligands bonded, so co-ordination number 4.

Balance charges for oxidation number**
Let Pt oxidation number be $x$. For the cation: $x + 4(0) + 2(-1) = +2$, so $x = +4$. For the anion: $x + 4(-1) = -2$, so $x = +2$. Notice $\text{NH}_3$ is neutral and never changes the charge balance, while each $\text{Cl}^-$ contributes -1.

Final answer: $[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]^{2+}$: co-ordination number = 6, oxidation number of Pt = +4
$[\text{PtCl}_4]^{2-}$: co-ordination number = 4, oxidation number of Pt = +2

hints: Recall that a 6 co-ordinate Pt(IV) complex is octahedral, so place Pt at the centre with four $\text{NH}_3$ in a plane and two $\text{Cl}$ positions to vary.
Think how the two identical $\text{Cl}$ ligands can be arranged, either opposite each other at 180 degrees or adjacent at 90 degrees.
walkthrough:
Set up the octahedral framework**
With co-ordination number 6 this must be octahedral. Put $\text{Pt}$ in the centre. A good way to draw it is four ligands in a square plane around Pt, one above and one below. Use normal lines for in plane, a solid wedge for coming out, and a hashed wedge for going back.

Place the trans isomer**
For trans, put the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands directly opposite, for example one at the top and one at the bottom of the octahedron, with the four $\text{NH}_3$ forming the square plane in the middle. The $\text{Cl-Pt-Cl}$ angle is $180^{\circ}$.

Place the cis isomer**
For cis, put the two $\text{Cl}$ ligands next to each other, for example one at the top and one on the side, with $\text{NH}_3$ occupying the other four positions. The $\text{Cl-Pt-Cl}$ angle is $90^{\circ}$. Label $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NH}_3$ clearly on each diagram.

Final answer: Octahedral diagrams with Pt at centre:
trans-$[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]^{2+}$: two $\text{Cl}$ opposite each other (180 degrees apart).
cis-$[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]^{2+}$: two $\text{Cl}$ adjacent (90 degrees apart).
Both drawn in 3D with solid wedge, hashed wedge and straight bonds to show octahedral shape.

hints: Identify which halide is free in solution as a counter ion and which is locked inside the complex in each compound.
Recall the reagent that precipitates free $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{Br}^-$ and the different colours of the two silver halide precipitates.
walkthrough:
Separate inside from outside the brackets**
Anything inside the square brackets is co-ordinately bonded to Pt and will not come off in water. Anything outside is a free counter ion. So $[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]\text{Br}_2$ releases $2\text{Br}^-$ into solution, while $[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Br}_2]\text{Cl}_2$ releases $2\text{Cl}^-$ into solution. That is the key difference you can test for.

Apply the classic halide test**
Add dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ to remove interfering ions, then $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$. The reactions are $\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Br}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgBr}(s)$ cream, and $\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)$ white. So the first compound gives cream and the second gives white, giving a positive identification of each.

Final answer: Test: add dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ followed by aqueous $\text{AgNO}_3$.
$[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Cl}_2]\text{Br}_2$: cream precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$.
$[\text{Pt}(\text{NH}_3)_4\text{Br}_2]\text{Cl}_2$: white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$.
Only ionic halide outside the complex precipitates, co-ordinated halide does not react.

hints: Remember that square planar $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ can show cis and trans but a planar shape can never be chiral.
Consider why a tetrahedral complex with only two types of ligand, $\text{M}\text{A}_2\text{B}_2$, has a plane of symmetry and cannot show either type.

Focus on the octahedral complex with two bidentate $\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ ligands, which can form cis and trans forms and the cis form is non superimposable on its mirror image.
walkthrough:
Check the octahedral bis(ethylenediamine) complex**
$\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ is 1,2-diaminoethane, a bidentate ligand. $[\text{Co}(en)_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ can have the two $\text{Cl}$ opposite (trans) or adjacent (cis), so geometrical isomerism occurs. The cis form has no plane of symmetry and exists as a pair of non superimposable mirror images, so optical isomerism also occurs. Overall answer is both.

Check the square planar complex**
Square planar $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_2\text{Cl}_2]^{2-}$ is of type $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$. It can have $\text{CN}$ groups cis or trans to each other, so geometrical isomerism occurs. However all square planar molecules are flat and therefore achiral with a mirror plane, so no optical isomerism is possible.

Check the tetrahedral complex**
Tetrahedral $[\text{CuBr}_2\text{Cl}_2]^{2-}$ has only two ligand types arranged tetrahedrally. Any arrangement is identical by rotation, there is no cis trans distinction as all bond angles are $109.5^{\circ}$, and the molecule has planes of symmetry so it is not chiral. Therefore neither type is shown.

Final answer: octahedral $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2)_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$: both
square planar $[\text{Ni}(\text{CN})_2\text{Cl}_2]^{2-}$: geometrical
tetrahedral $[\text{CuBr}_2\text{Cl}_2]^{2-}$: neither

hints: Start with the shape relationship between the substrate molecule and the hollow in the enzyme where it binds.
Describe what happens when the substrate enters that site to form the intermediate complex and how bonds in the substrate are affected.
Finish by explaining how products leave and how the energy barrier is lowered so the enzyme is unchanged.
walkthrough:
Show specific binding**
Draw the enzyme as a large shape with a hollow active site that exactly matches the shape of the substrate, like a lock and key. Label enzyme, active site and substrate. The point to make is that the substrate shape is complementary to the active site, so only the correct substrate fits. It is held by intermolecular forces, hydrogen bonds and ionic interactions.

Form the enzyme substrate complex**
Draw the substrate sitting inside the active site to make the ES complex. Once bound, the enzyme strains the substrate and weakens specific covalent bonds. In a metalloenzyme the transition metal ion in the active site can co-ordinately bond to the substrate and polarise it, making it more reactive.

Release products and regenerate enzyme**
Draw the breakdown products leaving the active site, with the free enzyme ready for the next cycle. Explain that an alternative pathway of lower activation energy, $E_{\text{A}}$, is provided, so breakdown is much faster at body temperature while the enzyme itself is unchanged.

Final answer: Substrate shape is complementary to the enzyme active site.
Substrate binds / fits into the active site to form an enzyme substrate complex, bonds in substrate are weakened.
Reaction occurs with lower $E_{\text{A}}$, products are released leaving enzyme unchanged.
Suitably labelled diagram showing enzyme, active site, substrate, enzyme substrate complex and enzyme + products.
